cf.title: Don't close relation files when the visibility map is extended

input.subject: Don't close relation files when the visibility map is extended

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal: message #1 reports a production stall with numbers and message #2 reproduces the cost independently. The remaining points are fixable design questions. maintenance-fit-1 asks for the rule that makes the size-only message safe, and replication-ondisk-1 asks whether the new message ID can reach WAL and which branches are targeted. Both need a committer who knows the smgr and sinval code, and the thread has only two messages.

brief.title: Send a fork-size-only invalidation when the visibility map is extended
brief.problem: When vm_extend() grows the visibility map it sends an smgr invalidation, and every backend with the relation open closes all its segment files and reopens them later. On filesystems where open() is costly, such as encryption layers, this stalls inserts on large tables while VACUUM or on-access pruning extends the map.
brief.proposed_design: The patch adds a new shared invalidation message that only resets the cached fork sizes, and vm_extend() sends it instead of the full smgr invalidation. Backends keep their files open and see new map pages when they do today. The author rejected dropping the invalidation, because a backend that does not prune the pages keeps a stale map size until VACUUM finishes.
user_visible_surface: New shared invalidation message type in sinval.h.
New or changed C functions in inval.h and smgr.h for sending and handling the fork-size reset.
New invalidation message description in standbydesc.c, so pg_waldump output for standby or commit records can change.
author_claims: None of the file reopens caused by vm_extend() are needed; other backends only need to learn the new map size.
On eCryptfs with about 2,700 segments and 300 inserting clients, VACUUM caused about 10 million opens before and under 1 million after.
p99 insert latency during VACUUM dropped from about 350ms to under 20ms, and the extra system CPU mostly went away.
The same invalidation exists in every branch from 14 to master; check-world passes.
brief.thread_state: Jakub Wartak traced the invalidation to commit b4e074172768, reproduced high system CPU on encrypted filesystems, and asked whether Postgres should optimize for costly open() at all, since DDL invalidations cause the same load. The author's question about why the full invalidation is needed has no answer yet.
unclear: The material does not say whether the new message appears in WAL commit records, which would affect standbys running an older minor version if back-patched.
The author does not say whether he wants a back-patch to 14 or a master-only change.
The thread has no benchmark on ext4 or XFS showing no regression.
The proposal does not say whether any code path relied on vm_extend() closing files, for example after truncation or on a hot standby.
Two CommitFest entries exist: 7524 from the author and 7528 from Jakub Wartak.
search_queries: file descriptor open cost encrypted filesystem

objections.title: Second smgr invalidation kind that callers must choose correctly
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch that grows, truncates or rewrites a fork copies the vm_extend() call and sends the fork-size-only message. Backends then keep descriptors for segments that were removed, or keep other smgr state that a close used to reset. The result is a rare wrong-size or stale-file bug found in the field, not a test failure.
objections.argument: Today one smgr invalidation closes everything, so a caller cannot pick the wrong strength. The patch adds a weaker message that is safe only when no segment disappears and no other per-relation smgr state needs a reset, and the proposal does not state that rule anywhere a future author would see it. In [P1], removing an smgrclose() also skipped resetting smgr_cached_nblocks and set up a convention that smgrclose() may be left out in one special case. The same kind of convention appears here.
objections.author_must_show: What invariant makes the size-only message safe for vm_extend(), and where is it documented or asserted so a later caller cannot use it after truncation?

critic.reasoning: The proposal does not state the rule that makes the size-only message safe, and message #1 itself asks whether the full invalidation is needed. [P1] concerns duplicate smgrclose() calls after unlink and should not be used as support.

objections.title: New invalidation message type is unsafe to back-patch across minor versions
objections.failure_scenario: A user runs a primary on the patched minor release and a hot standby on the previous one. The primary writes a commit or XLOG_INVALIDATIONS record that carries the new message ID. The older standby has no handler for that ID, so replay or logical decoding errors out, and the user finds out when the standby stops applying WAL.
objections.argument: The patch touches standbydesc.c, which describes invalidation messages carried in WAL, so the new ID may be written to WAL records. Message #1 notes the problem exists in every branch from 14 to master. The proposal does not say whether it targets those branches or master only. It also does not say whether the new ID always stays out of WAL; vm_extend() sends its invalidation directly, but the material does not confirm the new ID never enters the transactional queue.
objections.author_must_show: Can the new message ID ever be written to WAL, and if so, is the patch meant for master only or for back-branches too?

critic.reasoning: The smgr invalidation is sent outside the transactional queue today, which suggests the new ID stays out of WAL. But the patch touches standbydesc.c and message #1 names branches 14 to master without stating a target, so the question stands.

objections.title: Point fix for one source of a general reopen cost
objections.failure_scenario: After this lands, the same encrypted-filesystem user still sees the inserts stall when DDL, truncation or other relcache and smgr invalidations hit a large table. Each source then gets its own special message, and the number of invalidation variants grows release by release.
objections.argument: Message #2 says DDL invalidations cause the same load and asks whether Postgres should optimize for costly open() at all. That question has no answer in the thread. A committer would likely ask whether the cost belongs at the smgr or fd layer, such as keeping descriptors across an invalidation when segments still exist, so that every invalidation source gains instead of one.
objections.author_must_show: Why is a vm_extend()-specific message better than making smgr invalidation keep open segments in general, and which other sources would still cause mass reopens?

critic.reasoning: Message #2 raises this question and the thread has no answer. It is weaker than stated, because vm_extend() fires routinely during VACUUM on large tables while DDL on them is rare, so a targeted fix may still be justified.

refuted.title: New sinval message type may not be safe to back-patch to 14
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator applies a minor release on the primary first, as the docs advise, while a standby or logical decoding consumer still runs the older minor. If the new message id ever reaches a WAL record, the older binary does not recognize the id and may stop with an error. The operator finds out when replication or decoding halts.
refuted.argument: Message #1 stresses that the same invalidation exists in 14 through master, which reads as a request to back-patch, but the proposal never says which branches it targets. The patch touches standbydesc.c, which describes invalidation messages carried in WAL, so the new id may be WAL-visible. Adding a sinval message id in a minor release has no precedent in this material. The proposal does not say whether the message stays local or how older readers handle it.
refuted.author_must_show: Is this master-only or a back-patch, and can the new message id ever appear in WAL read by an older-minor standby or logical decoder?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-1, which asks the same back-patch and WAL question and also notes that vm_extend() sends its invalidation directly.

refuted.title: Fix needs a new message type but the reporter runs 17
refuted.failure_scenario: The reported stall is on 17, so the patch helps the reporter only if it is back-patched. A back-patch adds a sinval message ID to stable branches. A server or standby on an older minor that receives the new ID, through WAL or any other path, raises an error for an unrecognized message instead of ignoring it.
refuted.argument: The patch touches sinval.h and standbydesc.c, so the new message has a WAL description and changes a struct used by extensions. Message #1 notes that the invalidation exists in 14 through master but does not say whether back-patching is intended. The proposal does not say whether the new message can appear in commit records replayed by a standby. A master-only fix leaves the reported user unhelped for years, and the shape of the patch looks hard to back-patch.
refuted.author_must_show: Is this master-only, and if not, how does a standby or extension on an older minor release handle the new invalidation message ID?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-1. The added point that a master-only fix does not help a user on 17 is true of any non-back-patched improvement and is not a design flaw.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: The patch touches standbydesc.c, which describes invalidation messages carried in WAL records.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a message type in sinval.h and changes declarations in smgr.h and inval.h.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: Message #1 reports the problem on 17 and names branches 14 to master, but states no target branch.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: A second, weaker smgr invalidation kind exists that later callers must choose correctly.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The patch changes what every backend does on receiving the invalidation that vm_extend() sends during VACUUM and pruning.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: Message #2 asks whether Postgres should optimize for filesystems with costly open() at all.

questions: What invariant makes it safe for other backends to keep their segment files open after vm_extend(), and where does the patch state or assert it?
Can the new message ID ever be written to a WAL record, such as a commit or XLOG_INVALIDATIONS record?
Is the patch meant for master only, or for back-branches down to 14?
Why is a vm_extend()-specific message better than making the smgr invalidation keep existing segments open in general, and which other sources would still cause mass reopens?
Does a benchmark on ext4 or XFS show no regression from the new message?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows the smgr and md layers and shared invalidation handling, including how invalidation messages reach WAL and standbys. No such committer has spoken in the two visible messages.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the claim that no backend needs its files closed when the visibility map grows, on primaries and standbys, for as long as the message type exists. A back-patch adds minor-version compatibility of the new message ID.
committability.author_follow_up: The author tested an alternative design and asked the list for the missing reason in message #1; no later sign either way.

priority.reason: The measured gain is large but shows on filesystems with costly open(), large tables and many writers; other users only lose unneeded reopens. The patch is small, about 10 KiB over seven files, but it adds a permanent invalidation kind in smgr and sinval code that needs expert review.

provisional_note: Without the code, nobody could check whether the new message stays out of the transactional invalidation queue, or whether any path relied on vm_extend() closing files. The reason for the standbydesc.c change is also unverified.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Remove duplicated smgrclose call
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes the smgrclose() calls that follow smgrdounlinkall() in smgrDoPendingDeletes() and similar places, since smgrdounlinkall() already closes the forks. On review it was split in two: one part removes the duplicate calls, the other makes smgrdounlinkall() call smgrclose() itself.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Masahiko Sawada found that removing smgrclose() after smgrdounlinkall() skips operations such as resetting smgr_cached_nblocks, and would create a convention that smgrclose() may be omitted only after smgrunlinkall(). He also saw little benefit compared to the risk, and rejected the author's alternative because smgrdounlinkall() would then call mdunlink() without mdclose(). Álvaro Herrera returned the entry and asked for one complete patch instead of two halves.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Also, I'm concerned that even if we could remove these
smgrclose() calls the benefit of removing these calls here would be
very small compared to the risk of changing the code.

precedents_retrieved.title: Use function smgrclose() to replace the loop
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch replaces the loops in smgrdestroy() and smgrdounlinkall() that call smgr_close() for each fork with a call to smgrclose(). It is a refactoring meant to remove duplicated code.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Ilia Evdokimov asked whether smgrclose() is equivalent to the loop, and Junwang Zhao noted that it also resets smgr_cached_nblocks[] and smgr_targblock but saw no harm. The author argued for the change in October 2024, and the thread has no later messages before the withdrawal in December 2025.

precedents_retrieved.title: Windows pg_basebackup unable to create >2GB pg_wal.tar tarballs ("could not close file: Invalid argument" when creating pg_wal.tar of size ~ 2^31 bytes)
precedents_retrieved.summary: On Windows, pg_basebackup in tar mode fails with "could not close file: Invalid argument" when pg_wal.tar grows past 2^31 bytes, because off_t, lseek() and ftruncate() are 32-bit there. A proof-of-concept patch redirects lseek() to _lseeki64() so the WAL tar file can exceed 2 GiB.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last message discusses how to back-patch the fix, including an ftruncate() replacement, and nobody objects to it. The entry was withdrawn three days later, and no message gives a reason.

precedents_retrieved.title: Use simplehash.h instead of dynahash in SMgr
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch replaces the dynahash table that smgr.c uses to look up SMgrRelation entries with a simplehash table, using a small entry that points to the SMgrRelationData, plus a custom hash function; it made recovery about 10% faster in the author's benchmark. Because simplehash does not keep pointers to entries stable, the author later replaced this with a new hash table implementation (generichash) that uses segments and bitmaps.
precedents_retrieved.objection: After the change to a new hash table implementation, Thomas Munro questioned adding another hash table and making the hash table provide fast iteration over its items. The author reports that Andres Freund also opposed the design, saying bitmaps are slow, but those messages are off-list and not shown. With no consensus and no update for two months, the patch no longer applied, and Michael Paquier marked it returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Thomas made it quite clear it's not for the patch, and on discussing the patch with Andres, it turned out he does not like the idea either.

This reverts commit fba105b1099f4f5fa7283bb17cba6fed2baa8d0c.
That approach had problems with the smgr-level state not tracking what
we really want to happen, and with the VFD-level state not tracking the
smgr-level state very well either.  In consequence, it was still possible
to hold kernel file descriptors open for long-gone tables (as in recent
report from Tore Halset), and yet there were also cases of FDs being closed
undesirably soon.  A replacement implementation will follow.

precedents_retrieved.title: warn if GUC set to an invalid shared library
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch emits a WARNING when ALTER SYSTEM, ALTER ROLE or ALTER DATABASE sets shared_preload_libraries, session_preload_libraries or local_preload_libraries to a library file that cannot be found, with a DETAIL saying the server or new sessions will fail to start. It also adds a CONTEXT line naming the setting and the config file line when startup fails on a missing library, and still allows setting the value before the library is installed.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author did not answer Heikki Linnakangas's November 2024 review, so the entry was returned with feedback after four weeks. That review asked for examples of what is accepted and when the warnings appear, and asked about documentation. It also noted that the new PGC_S_TEST_FUNCTION source was missing from GucSource_Names, and it suggested a separate is_testing flag as another design. Robert Haas and Heikki both said the thread needed too much context to review, and an earlier step that switched ALTER SYSTEM to PGC_S_TEST was dropped because it would let invalid values into postgresql.auto.conf.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
All this feedback was 4 weeks ago, and is unanswered, so I've marked
the CF entry as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Windows filesystem support improvements
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a small C TAP framework for unit-testing low-level code without a server, plus tests of the src/port Windows filesystem wrappers. Explicitly request Windows 10 POSIX unlink and rename semantics through SetFileInformationByHandle(), based on Victor Spirin's earlier patch, with fallback code where unsupported.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew it. Explicit POSIX semantics work on NTFS, but ReFS and SMB do not support them, and nothing in CI or the build farm tests those filesystems. The tree would then gain code that breaks on them, which amounts to dropping support, and no non-POSIX code could be removed unless the project declared SMB and ReFS unsupported.

precedents_retrieved.title: Unified file access using virtual file descriptors
precedents_retrieved.summary: Make virtual file descriptors (VFDs) the common interface for most non-buffer-cache, non-WAL files, adding sequential read/write, seek/tell, append and ferror-style error calls to fd.c. A second patch converts many callers from system or C library file calls to VFDs, as groundwork for transparent encryption, compression or checksums.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch failed to compile on CFbot (an undeclared MAXIMUM_VFD in fd.c), and the author did not post a new version after this was reported. The commitfest manager returned it with feedback for that reason, and no design review appears in the thread.

precedents_retrieved.title: Write visibility map during CLUSTER/VACUUM FULL
precedents_retrieved.summary: Make CLUSTER and VACUUM FULL write the visibility map during heap rewrite, by having rewriteheap.c build VM pages alongside heap pages (bypassing the buffer manager) and flush them to smgr. It used its own simplified all-visible check, relying on HeapTupleSatisfiesVacuum() having already set hint bits; TOAST relations were left without a VM.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund objected to copying visibility-map implementation details into rewriteheap.c and to adding another copy of visibility-determination logic, which he said has proven hard to get right. He also questioned part of the motivation and pointed to related prior discussion that might share logic, especially for TOAST. The author did not respond to these comments for over two months, and the entry was marked returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I don't think we should have yet another copy of logic determining
visibility. It has repeatedly proven hard to get right in the past, and
it'll not get better by having yet another copy.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent proposed this idea, and P1's reason does not carry over because this patch still resets the cached fork sizes. Message #2 says commit b4e074172768 first sent this invalidation to fix a regression, but it reports no reason that the files must be closed.
The proposal changes no SQL, GUC, catalog, pg_dump or psql surface. The only user-visible changes are pg_waldump text and the back-patch question above.
The patch changes no on-disk format. Visibility map extension during standby replay runs its own invalidation in the startup process, so the standby keeps today's behaviour.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. It changes an internal shared invalidation message that only the server sends, adds no SQL surface, function, setting or view, and exposes nothing new to unprivileged users. It reduces file-open load rather than adding a denial-of-service path. The risk that a back-patched new message type in commit records reaches an older standby is a compatibility question for the replication and backpatch angle.
Objections found; the change itself removes work for all users, so no hot-path objection is raised.

Postgres has no existing way to tell other backends a fork grew without making them close their files. The only cross-backend message for this is the full smgr invalidation that the patch replaces, and no extension or hook can change what vm_extend() sends. The new message is a narrower form of an existing mechanism, so it is not a second way to do the same job. Whether it is safe and wanted is for the design and desirability angles to judge.

The material shows real demand. Message #1 reports a production stall on a 4TB partition on 17, with numbers, and Jakub Wartak independently reproduced high system CPU on encrypted filesystems in message #2, naming three such Linux filesystems. The change also drops unneeded file reopens for every user, so the cost does not fall mainly on non-users. Jakub's broader question about other sinvals is a scope question, not missing demand.
